How robust is a disparity estimate?

Mustapha Mohammed, Sarah Hamed, Souci Frissa, Aisha Mohamed and Nathan Stanley, Black Thrive Global

23 October 2026

Source: vignettes/robustness.Rmd
robustness.Rmd

A stop-rate ratio is a simple number built on several choices and on data that are incomplete in known ways. This vignette shows how BlackThriveSS lets you ask, for any force, year and group, which conclusions survive those choices and which depend on them. Everything below runs offline from the bundled release, and every table and chart can be saved and replayed.

Three kinds of uncertainty are kept apart throughout:

  • Sampling variability: the 95% Poisson intervals on the recorded counts, and the rank intervals from redrawing those counts.
  • Missing ethnicity: stops with no recorded ethnic group are excluded from every ratio. The allocation range reports the ratio under the two extreme allocations of those stops, which bound every other allocation.
  • Missing returns: months a force did not submit are missing, never zero, and counts are never annualised. Coverage is reported beside every comparison.

The package does not combine these into one number, because they answer different questions.

Bounds under unknown ethnicity 

x <- btg_get_data()
s <- btg_sensitivity(x)
head(s[c("force_label", "unknown_share", "ratio", "ratio_min", "ratio_max", "parity_direction")])
force_label unknown_share ratio ratio_min ratio_max parity_direction
Norfolk 0.0306076 9.971068 9.616471 13.788563 above
Devon & Cornwall 0.0394330 9.748324 9.336930 20.940844 above
West Mercia 0.0443350 9.673906 9.134508 16.137257 above
Sussex 0.0104720 9.461250 9.338614 10.414488 above
Surrey 0.0169252 8.612550 8.419686 9.743609 above
Dorset 0.2204675 8.217899 6.250789 51.673153 above 
table(s$parity_direction, useNA = "ifany")
#> 
#> above  <NA> 
#>    40     4

ratio_min counts every unknown-ethnicity stop as White and ratio_max counts every one as Black; allocating them in the same proportions as the recorded stops would leave the ratio unchanged. parity_direction says whether the whole range sits above or below 1, or whether the side of parity depends on the unknown stops. The range can be wide where a group’s resident population is small, and that is the finding, not a defect.

btg_plot_sensitivity(x)

The same question for a comparison close to parity:

y <- btg_get_data("force_ethnicity_year")
btg_plot_sensitivity(y, year = 2024, group = "Asian", ranking = "closest")

How certain is a rank?

A league-table position is far less certain than the ratio behind it. The rank interval redraws each eligible force’s counts from Poisson distributions with the recorded counts as means and re-ranks every draw; the seed is fixed and the caller’s random number state is restored.

r <- btg_rank_stability(x, draws = 500)
head(r[c("force_label", "ratio", "rank", "rank_lower", "rank_upper", "prob_top")], 12)
force_label ratio rank rank_lower rank_upper prob_top
Norfolk 9.971068 1 1 6 1.000
Devon & Cornwall 9.748324 2 1 7 1.000
West Mercia 9.673906 3 1 6 1.000
Sussex 9.461250 4 1 6 1.000
Surrey 8.612550 5 3 9 0.994
Dorset 8.217899 6 1 18 0.704
Nottinghamshire 8.105919 7 5 12 0.918
Cumbria 8.046936 8 3 17 0.712
Warwickshire 7.821879 9 3 19 0.648
Suffolk 7.655695 10 5 17 0.546
Cambridgeshire 7.573837 11 6 17 0.490
Lincolnshire 7.518498 12 4 20 0.450

rank_best and rank_worst in btg_sensitivity() answer the other question: how far every force’s unknown stops could move the rank if they were allocated for or against it.

head(s[s$eligible, c("force_label", "rank", "rank_best", "rank_worst")], 8)

Across every year and group

For a study rather than a single chart, run the same functions over the full force table. btg_sensitivity() returns one row per force, year and group, with ranks and bounds within each year and group.

all <- btg_sensitivity(y)
settled <- all[all$eligible, ]
with(settled, table(group, parity_direction))
#>        parity_direction
#> group   above below sensitive
#>   Asian   258    14        80
#>   Black   349     0         3
#>   Mixed    51     4        21
#>   Other   220     4       121
aggregate(unknown_share ~ year, data = all[all$group == "Black", ], FUN = median)
year unknown_share
2018 0.0499212
2019 0.0563725
2020 0.0510737
2021 0.0579127
2022 0.0648038
2023 0.0637218
2024 0.0490643
2025 0.0512245
2026 0.0616438

Rank stability over several years and groups is one call; keep draws modest for exploratory work and raise it for a final table.

stable <- btg_rank_stability(btg_get_data("force_ethnicity_year", years = 2023:2025, groups = "Black"), draws = 300)
aggregate(cbind(width = rank_upper - rank_lower) ~ year, data = stable, FUN = median)
year width
2023 7
2024 6
2025 7

btg_robustness_summary() puts the counts a study needs in one table: one row per year and group, with the number of forces, how many meet the display rule, how many of those keep their side of parity under every allocation, the unknown share, the typical width of a rank interval, how many top-ten places are settled and how many forces have full-year returns.

btg_robustness_summary(btg_get_data("force_ethnicity_year", years = 2023:2025), draws = 300)

Has the source moved on?

The snapshot is fixed, but Police.uk keeps publishing. btg_source_status() reads the source’s availability feed, which lists for each month the forces whose stop and search data are present, and reports newer months and any force-month inside the snapshot’s verified window that has since been added or withdrawn. It is the package’s only use of the network and returns NULL with a message when the feed cannot be read, so it is not run here.

status <- btg_source_status()
status
status$changes

A late addition or a withdrawal is a reason to build a new release, never to edit this one; the proposal’s audit of revisions across releases starts from exactly this comparison.

Change over time, with coverage attached

btg_change() compares each area’s ratio in two years, with an interval on the ratio of ratios and the coverage of both years. A change between a complete year and an incomplete one is not a change in policing.

ch <- btg_change(btg_get_data("force_ethnicity_year", groups = "Black"))
table(ch$change_direction, useNA = "ifany")
#> 
#>  higher unclear    <NA> 
#>       9      31       4
head(ch[ch$change_direction %in% c("higher", "lower"),
        c("force_label", "ratio_from", "ratio_to", "change", "change_lower", "change_upper", "comparable_coverage")])
force_label ratio_from ratio_to change change_lower change_upper comparable_coverage

Reproduce and share

Every chart carries its table and a saved view. The view pins the release, its checksums, the selection and the settings; it contains no code.

p <- btg_plot_sensitivity(y, year = 2024, group = "Asian", ranking = "closest")
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
btg_save_view(p, path)
replay <- btg_from_view(path)
stopifnot(identical(btg_figure_data(replay), btg_figure_data(p)))
unlink(path)

btg_export() writes a dataset to CSV with a JSON sidecar recording the release, checksums, selection, citation and limitations, so that a file sent on still says where its numbers came from.

csv <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
files <- btg_export(btg_get_data("force_ethnicity_year", years = 2025, groups = "Black"), csv)
basename(files)
#> [1] "file1d8b61d2c66f.csv"          "file1d8b61d2c66f.json"        
#> [3] "file1d8b61d2c66f-coverage.csv"
unlink(files)

Methods in one place

Every quantity above is computed from four recorded numbers per area, year and group: the group’s recorded stops g, the White recorded stops w, and the Census 2021 resident populations P_g and P_w; u is the number of recorded stops with no recorded ethnicity.

  • Rate per 1,000 residents: 1000 * g / P_g and 1000 * w / P_w.
  • Ratio: (g / P_g) / (w / P_w), withheld when w is zero or the populations are not comparable.
  • 95% interval: exp(log(ratio) ± 1.96 * sqrt(1/g + 1/w)), for positive counts. It treats both counts as independent Poisson counts with fixed denominators.
  • Allocation range: ratio_min = (g / P_g) / ((w + u) / P_w) and ratio_max = ((g + u) / P_g) / (w / P_w). For any split of the unknown stops between the two groups, with the remainder in other groups, the ratio lies between them.
  • Rank bounds: a force’s best rank is one plus the number of other eligible forces whose ratio_min exceeds its ratio_max; its worst rank is one plus the number whose ratio_max exceeds its ratio_min.
  • Rank interval: draw g* ~ Poisson(g) and w* ~ Poisson(w) for every eligible force, rank the simulated ratios, repeat draws times, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of each force’s rank; prob_top is the share of draws in which the force ranks within the top top.
  • Change between years: ratio_to / ratio_from with the interval exp(log(change) ± 1.96 * sqrt(1/g_1 + 1/w_1 + 1/g_2 + 1/w_2)).

Eligibility and ranks follow the dashboard’s display rule: a positive finite ratio from at least 200 stops with known ethnicity and comparable resident populations (White residents of at least 50,000, and neither British Transport Police nor City of London). The audit in btg_validate() checks that the stored ratios, intervals and ranks reproduce these calculations.

What these tools do not do

They do not adjust for who is present in an area, impute missing returns, forecast populations past Census 2021, or reconcile officer-defined with self-reported ethnicity. They do not say whether a disparity is discriminatory. They make the evidence, and its limits, explicit enough to argue about.
